tagline.text: The ruins of a 1595 Dominican mission church beside the northern Cagayan coastal highway

location.label: Location
location.text: Sitio Nagsimbaanan, Barangay Namuac, Sanchez Mira, Cagayan (halfway between Sanchez Mira and Claveria)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,200 (daily transport from Tuguegarao or Laoag; confirm any entrance fee locally)

children.text: Pata Church Ruins mark the site of an early Cagayan Valley mission church founded by Dominican missionaries in 1595. They stand beside the national highway between Sanchez Mira and Claveria, where brick walls and column bases survive among the grass.

Pata Church Ruins are the remains of a Dominican church on the northern coast of Cagayan, roughly halfway between the town centers of Sanchez Mira and Claveria. Wikipedia records that the church was built on June 15, 1595, and names Fray Gaspar Zarfate and Fray Miguel de San Jacinto as the friars who supervised construction. Locally the spot is called Nagsimbaanan, and it is presented as a historic site managed by the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP). Unlike the famous large church ruins elsewhere in the Philippines, it is a quiet ruin with almost no visitor facilities. It is easy to reach, only a short walk on a dirt path from the highway.

It is known as one of the earliest mission centers in the Cagayan Valley. According to archaeological records, the church was first built with light materials, then rebuilt in stone and brick, and dedicated to Saint Mary Magdalene. Old maps from the 1890s already show it as a ruin, so it was clearly abandoned long ago. One photo caption says the Pata community lost importance once Aparri became the main port of entry to the Cagayan Valley. Few records explain how the church fell into ruin, and a village legend says a bell was so loud that the neighbors destroyed the church. This story has not been confirmed, so treat it as an interesting piece of oral tradition only.

What remains today are sections of walls built of stone and red brick, the altar-side wall, a broken column, and brick flooring. There is no roof or door, vines and grass cover the walls, and treasure-hunting pits have reportedly dug up the ground. In July 2025 a team from the University of the Philippines School of Archaeology excavated the site and found brick floors, column bases, graves, and pieces of 15th- to 19th-century porcelain. The land is owned by the Archdiocese of Tuguegarao.

It suits travelers interested in early Spanish colonial history and northern Luzon road trips more than those looking for dramatic sights. It works well as a short stop on a coastal road journey that starts in Pagudpud, passes the Patapat Viaduct and crosses into Cagayan. Plan it as a stop of 1–2 hours rather than a place to stay long.

blocks.title: Site of a 1595 Dominican mission church

children.text: It is known as one of the earliest churches in the Cagayan Valley. The marker is also said to record that Dominican friars built it on June 15, 1595.
Walls of red brick and stone bound with lime mortar stand among the grass. There is no roof, but walking along the lines where the walls once stood lets you judge the size of the chapel.
Archaeological work confirmed the altar-side wall and a brick column base. The report says the building ran north to south, with a nave divided into two aisles.
Surveys found that a convent and sacristy stood on the east side of the building. Traces of brick floors and stone steps remain, showing that this was not just a chapel but a mission base.

The University of the Philippines School of Archaeology excavated the site. The 15th- to 19th-century porcelain, roof tiles, and bricks it found show that the area was a long-standing setting for trade and daily life.

blocks.title: View over the Pata River delta

children.text: The ruins sit on a rise that juts toward the Pata River delta, and a tributary of the river reaches the site on its east side. Grass, river, and open sky toward the sea come together in one scene, which makes for quiet photographs.

blocks.title: Statue of Mary and Holy Week pilgrims

children.text: A statue of the Virgin Mary was installed in 2016, and devotees are said to visit on religious occasions such as Holy Week. At other times visitors are few and the place is peaceful.

The survey report explains that the building went through three phases: an early structure of light materials, a stone phase, and a phase clad in brick with rubble infill. It is rewarding to look for the different materials within the same wall.

items.title: Same-day stop route
items.subtitle: A roadside visit between Sanchez Mira and Claveria

children.text: Have breakfast in Sanchez Mira town and pick up water and snacks. There are reportedly no shops or restrooms around the ruins, so take care of these in town.
Take a tricycle or your own car along the highway for about
10km
to Barangay Namuac. Look for the arch marked Nagsimbaanan.
Pass through the bamboo gate behind the arch and follow the dirt path to the ruins. Greet the caretaker who lives in the house near the entrance and ask first whether you may look around.
Start at the southern entrance and walk clockwise: the belfry site to the west, the altar-side wall, then the convent area to the east. Do not climb on the walls or touch the bricks.
Take photos while looking toward the Pata River tributary, tidy up, then head to Claveria or Sanchez Mira for lunch.
Because the site is by the road, you do not need much time. The most efficient plan is to treat it as a midway stop on a day when you travel along the northern coastal road.

items.title: History route
items.subtitle: Following the early Cagayan mission churches

children.text: Start from Tuguegarao and see churches and ruins in the main towns of the Cagayan Valley. Visiting other church ruins in the region first, such as the Camalaniugan Church Ruins, gives you something to compare.
Arrive in Sanchez Mira, have lunch, and rest in preparation for the afternoon.
Study the wall structure and column bases at Pata Church Ruins. The sun is high at this hour and it is hot, so a hat and water are needed.
Head toward Claveria or toward Laoag. It is safer to pass along the highway before dark.
This route involves a lot of travel, so do not try to see everything in one day; consider basing yourself in Sanchez Mira or Claveria.
Domestic flights from Manila to Tuguegarao (TUG) operate at certain times, and schedules and airlines change often, so check before departure.
If you approach from the northwest, you can also fly from Manila to Laoag (LAO) and continue overland through Pagudpud into Cagayan.
There is no direct public transport from the airport to the ruins, so first travel to Sanchez Mira or Claveria.
Long-distance buses run from Manila toward Tuguegarao, Laoag, and Pagudpud, and the northern coastal highway continues along that route.
Bus schedules and fares vary by company and season, so check at the terminal or with the company.
If you board a bus or van toward Sanchez Mira or Claveria, ask the conductor in advance whether you can be dropped off near Namuac at the midpoint.
Travel along the highway between Sanchez Mira and Claveria and you will reach the ruins' entrance roughly halfway. The drive between the two town centers is said to take about
20 minutes
Hiring a tricycle for a round trip is the simplest option; negotiate the fare and agree on waiting time.
If you drive your own or a rented car, enter the coordinates 18.6142, 121.1606 into a map app. It is beside the road and easy to spot, but the arch may be small, so drive slowly.
Road surfaces and transport conditions change often, so check the latest situation locally.

Because this is an open-air site, the best time is when it is not raining. Northern Luzon is generally dry from November to April, but the northern Cagayan coast can be affected by monsoons and typhoons.

In the rainy season in particular, dirt paths turn muddy and the grass grows thick, so the walls may be hard to see. During Holy Week devotees visit, which changes the atmosphere but can mean more people.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Easiest time to walk, and the grass is moderate so the wall structure is easy to see.
There is almost no shade at midday, so early morning or late afternoon is recommended.
Dirt paths are muddy, the grass is overgrown, and getting around can be inconvenient.

items.label: Entrance fee
items.note: No official entrance fee information was found. Some introductions say it is free, but it is best to ask the caretaker directly.

items.label: Donation
items.note: A token of thanks to the people who look after the site.

items.label: Tricycle (round trip from town)
items.note: Negotiate, including waiting time; varies with distance and season

items.label: Bus or van fare
items.note: Varies by departure point and company, so check at the terminal

items.label: Lunch
items.note: At restaurants in Sanchez Mira or Claveria town

items.label: Lodging
items.note: Small town guesthouses; varies by season

items.label: Water and snacks
items.note: Reportedly no shops near the ruins, so buy supplies in town

There are reportedly no restaurants or lodgings near the ruins. It is realistic to eat and sleep in Sanchez Mira or Claveria town. Both are small towns, so expect small guesthouses and eateries rather than large hotels, and because businesses may change their operating status over time, contact them before you go.

If your schedule is longer, you could stay a night in Pagudpud and cross toward Cagayan in the morning. Eating at a seafood restaurant on the northern Ilocos coast and then moving on lets you see the ruins before lunch.
Prepare water, snacks, a hat, and sunscreen in town before you go. The ruins reportedly have little shade and no restroom.
Greet the caretaker who lives near the entrance first and tell them you are visiting. It is better still to get permission to take photos.
Do not take bricks or stones away or step on the walls. The old walls are weak and can collapse from a small impact.
Wear long trousers and shoes that cover your ankles. There is plenty of grass and vine, and treasure-hunting pits may remain in the ground.
If you use a tricycle, agree on a price that includes waiting time and ask the driver to take you back.
Combining this with other nearby church ruins, such as Camalaniugan Church Ruins, lets you compare the early mission history of Cagayan.
Holy Week may bring crowds or a different atmosphere because of religious events, so check the latest schedule.
Keep stories you hear locally separate from facts confirmed in records. Many tales, like the bell legend, have no documentation.
The site is known mainly for individual visits, so if you plan a group visit or filming, ask the tourism office of the Sanchez Mira municipal hall in advance.
This is a ruin with almost no safety fences or signs, so do not go close to the walls or climb them, and look around carefully.
The old brick walls may be cracked. Do not linger under them or lean on them.
Pits may be hidden in the grass, so watch your footing as you walk.
There are reportedly no facilities near the ruins, so bring your own water and basic first-aid supplies.
It is next to the highway, with frequent traffic. Take care when crossing the road or parking.
Opening hours and permission to enter may change, so check the latest announcements.
A coastal viaduct in northern Ilocos Norte on the way into Cagayan. Travel times depend on traffic, so check locally.
A beach town in northern Ilocos, a good place to spend a night before or after crossing into Cagayan.
The provincial capital of Cagayan, with an airport, and a base for visiting other church ruins and churches.
The nearest base for lodging and meals, reached along the highway.
A town west of the ruins, which can be visited together with Sanchez Mira as a base.
